extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate leaders, and students of public opinion/PR
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and standards for the practice of public relations counsel: how to study and gauge public opinion, create circumstances, choose media and advise clients on actions and policy to shape public sentiment. Emphasis is on both communicative tactics and substantive changes in client behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is the aggregate result of individual judgments; it is vague, mercurial and changeable and must be understood by going back to the individual who makes up the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that public opinion is built from many settled but often irrational individual judgments (religion, politics, habits). Counsel must account for dogmatic, authority-based, and culturally rooted beliefs when designing campaigns. Examples: differing egg color preferences by city; entrenched views on prohibition or spiritualism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a student of the public mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is first of all a student; his field of study is the public mind and his textbooks are the facts of life—press, advertisements, sermons, gossip, theater patter, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously listen to and study diverse sources (newspapers, billboards, speeches, everyday conversation) to detect trends and sentiments. Develop sensitivity comparable to clinical judgment in medicine. Example: counselors often have newspaper training to sense public likes and dislikes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research campaigns, surveys and symposia to gauge opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the practical means of gauging the public mind which modern advertising has developed: research campaigns, symposia, and surveys of particular groups or states of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these methods as confirmation or modification of intuitive appraisals. Use surveys to test reactions before wide rollout; combine qualitative listening with quantitative measures. Example: the text cites surveys and symposiums as instruments for confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances and events
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the primary instruments of the counsel is the creation of circumstances and events which help shape public attention and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan and stage events, productions or public occurrences (plays, parades, exhibitions) that dramatize and make accessible the client's message. Example: production of 'Damaged Goods' to overcome prudishness; parades and pamphlets for Lithuania to build international sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a wide range of communication instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast facts and ideas through advertising, motion pictures, circular letters, booklets, handbills, speeches, meetings, parades, news articles, magazine articles and any other mediums available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select from many media channels rather than relying on a single format; tailor channels to audience and goal. Example: counsel may advise one client to announce price changes by telegraph, another by circular, another by advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select communication medium tailored to client and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Different clients need different means to communicate the same underlying action; choice of medium (telegraph, circular, advertising, publication) should match the client, message and public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the public's expectations and the client's image when choosing format. Examples in text: announce by telegraph vs circular; publish a Bible vs a book of French tales; use prices in advertising for one store and not for another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise on client action and policy, not only messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel's role is increasingly to advise on actions and policies—modify client behavior to conform to public taste or to forestall adverse reaction—not merely to shape publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend substantive changes (e.g., withdraw hat-check privilege, change factory hygienic practices, found scholarships, exhibit wares in museums) as part of a public relations strategy. The counsel must keep clients from drifting into harmful situations by recommending policy changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret the public to the client and the client to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Act both as interpreter of the public mind for the client and as pleader interpreting the client’s case to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance internal advising (what the public thinks and will accept) with external advocacy (how to present the client). Serve as intermediary between client and press; decide what facts and impressions should be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain close relations with the press and journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the press is the greatest single medium for reaching the public mind, the counsel must have close contacts with journalists and understand newsroom practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage newspaper experience to predict what will be reported and how; provide timely communiques and manage reporters' expectations (examples include the Versailles press-room behavior). Hire press agents when discretion over reporting is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive to state-of-mind, geography and cultural tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitiveness to the state of mind of the public is difficult but essential; differences in locality, community and social circumstance affect opinion and receptiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for regional tastes (e.g., Boston vs New York egg color), community norms (resistance to prohibition), and situational contexts when crafting messages and recommending actions. Develop this sensitivity through experience and listening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate and organize disparate interests for unified appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: When members of diverse groups share a passive sentiment, form non-partisan committees or coalitions to make a united, articulate appeal that dramatizes unified support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring together representatives from varied affiliations to produce a visible, dramatic expression of unified opinion (example: meeting of women from diverse groups to support the League of Nations). Use coalitions to convert diffuse sympathy into organized pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity as public education to change attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity can be used to educate the public about the social, industrial or political importance of an issue or industry, thereby changing attitudes and behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design informative, accurate campaigns to stimulate demand, forecast behavior, and correct misconceptions (examples: Hoover’s publicity for coal, jewelers educating about value of jewelry, Lithuania’s pamphlets and motion pictures). Emphasize facts and constructive messaging to build understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build cooperative public spirit and good will
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should aim to create a cooperative spirit between client and public by offering helpful services and aligning client actions with public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiatives can include cooperating with community committees, arranging special travel facilities, aiding conventions, distributing helpful literature, or running educational programs (examples: New York Central cooperating with Welcome Stranger Committee; Health Department’s publicity for disease prevention). Use constructive programs to improve reputation and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish counsel from the old 'publicity man' (professional standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'counsel on public relations' differs from the old publicity man; counsel is a professional adviser who prevents drifting into harmful situations and pursues constructive public good rather than merely getting 'something for nothing' from publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uphold professional responsibility: advise on policy, create circumstances intelligently, and avoid purely ingratiating promotional tactics. The counsel should live up to the potential of the title by acting constructively and ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor changing conditions and adapt policies accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel must be alive to events of the day and advise clients to modify policies according to changes in public point of view and environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously monitor news, street conversation, organizational shifts and wartime/post-war conditions; recommend policy adjustments to align with lowered expectations or changed standards (example: telephone company explaining lowered wartime service standards to the public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity to protect clients from unfair criticism by providing accurate information
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative publicity can protect the majority of operators from unfair criticism by making salient facts known (example: publishing ratio of production to capacity to hold down over-expansion criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent, factual communications to put minority failures in context and shape reasonable public judgments. Use statistics and explanatory material to forestall misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as constructive force in the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, the public relations consultant is a constructive force whose results accelerate interest in matters valuable to social, economic or political life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue campaigns that not only benefit clients commercially but also contribute to public welfare—public education on health, industry importance, or civic attractions (examples: Health Department's campaigns; states promoting tourism).
